utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, assisted by Ruth Karper, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Administrative questions we have to discuss later, I think. As time is of the essence, we have to start immediately with our today witness, Mr. McLeod. Could he please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McLeod. You can hear me? Yes. Could you please be so kind and give the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And, please, be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We may start the examination of this witness in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Korner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, is your full name Charles George Alexander McLeod?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I think it's right that in 1992, you were working for an organisation called the -- as it was then called, the European Community Monitoring Mission, ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want just before I deal with some of the events that you covered in 1992, just to let the Trial Chamber a little bit about your background. I know you gave it all yesterday or the day before. I think it's right that, after leaving school, you joined the British army and were commissioned as a 2nd Lieutenant in September of 1982, in what was then the Queen's Regiment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you serve as a platoon commander in Germany and then on a short four-month operational tour in West Belfast, Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequently, did you go to university, where you read German?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was still in the territorial army during your university career?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you promoted whilst at university, and did you rejoin your battalion in 1987?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then go to Northern Ireland in 1988 for a period of two years?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you a battalion staff officer there and promoted to rank of captain?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think whilst you were there, you were -- I'm sorry, afterwards, you were awarded the MBE, Member of the Order of the British Empire, for your service in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you resign your commission and leave the army at the end of June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in July, were you appointed to ECMM as a monitor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In -- just so we can set the background, I think ECMM had had a base in Bosnia until about -- or had a mission in Bosnia until about May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then as a result of the death of one of its members, it pulled out?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It then, I think, went back in again in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you start making, as it were, overtures to the authorities in the Autonomous Region of Krajina towards the end of August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result, did you pay visits to Mr. Radic, the mayor of Banja Luka, beginning on the 20th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason for that being that other members of your team had had previous contacts with Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around this period, was there a conference, the London Conference, taking place, strangely enough, in London?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that had concluded, was it decided that there would be an international delegation sent to Bosnia with a view to inspecting, in particular, the camps which had recently been brought to the notice of the international public?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was a decision of the conference, but certainly at that time, the CSCE decided to send rapporteur missions to identify what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you asked to facilitate the particular mission that was headed by Sir John Thompson?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was planned to take place at the very end of August, the 30th and the 31st, in this particular area, the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as a result, did you go back and speak to Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then I think the actual mission started on the 30th of August, started by you going to Bosanska Gradiska, where there was a meeting with the mayor of Bosanska Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then did you go to Banja Luka from there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have a meeting with Mr. Radic and other people there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently pay a visit to the camp at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on the following day, did you go to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have a meeting there with a man who was -- or you described as the mayor of Banja Luka, Mr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Well, we met Mr. Stakic in Prijedor, as opposed to Banja Luka, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, did I say Banja Luka? You're quite right. Thank you. Did you keep notes of what was said at the meeting, not word for word, but the essence of what was being talked about?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And subsequently, did you prepare a report for the head of mission of ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you, please, to have your report in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If that could be handed up to the witness. I hope Your Honours have been provided with copies of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a report dated 23 August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's a report dated the 3rd of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Referring back to a meeting on the 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have several reports here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you prepared reports, just so we can deal with that, Mr. McLeod, you prepared reports on each of the meetings and, effectively, visits?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that had the 65 ter number of 349.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, before we go into the details, can I ask you this: Who was it that you wanted to meet or you were arranging for Sir John Thompson and others to meet? In other words, what function -- whatever they were called, whether it was mayor or president of municipality, what were you looking for in the people that you met?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The intention had been that Sir John would be able to meet the senior civilian and/or indeed, if they were available, military people who were in control of the territory. And so, as far as we were concerned, the meetings had been arranged for him to meet the senior civilian authorities in each of the areas that we went to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who had made those arrangements? Was it you or somebody else in ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It was ECMM that had done it. I can't remember exactly who the individual was who put together the programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we look, please, then at your report. We see in the introduction --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask, would Your Honour like me to read out all of it, or can I summarise some?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It depends. Has the Defence available also a version in B/C/S for the client?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. In this case, if the Defence so consents for facilitating the procedure, it seems not to be necessary to read out the entire report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see the introduction which was common to all your reports, stating where you had been. And then you say, in paragraph 2: "On the 31st of August, 1992, the team had a meeting with Dr. Stakic, the mayor of Prijedor, followed by a visit to the so-call 'open reception centre' at Trnopolje. I wrote detailed notes on much of what was said during the meetings, and this report on the meeting with Dr. Stakic is based on those notes." Then in paragraph 3, you set out the general points, only reporting in detail what was said, "by the people we met, not our sides." Then you explain that your notes, there may be gaps in it on conversations broken to general chat, and it's not a complete record of what was said. And then you deal with the conversations. "After the introductions, Dr. Stakic spoke." In the first free elections -- I'm sorry. Paragraph 4: "Dr. Stakic: In the first free elections since the Second World War, the Muslim party won the election and were in power for one and-a-half years, and they took the opportunity it gave them to arm the most extreme parts of the Muslim population. "This preparation has reached a culminating point at the end of April, beginning of May, when these armed groups put up barricades and when they started shameful murders of the army of Bosanska Krajina and the police. "As a result, the army and police cleared the barricades when they left Prijedor on the road to Banja Luka. And as soon as they left the city, the army and police were attacked, and three police and soldiers were killed. "In spite of our invitation to their representatives, religious leaders and well-known citizens, they did not come to talk to us. "And why have I mentioned the religious leaders? We found when we went to search the homes of religious leaders, we found U.S. made shotguns, which in the U.S. are forbidden for hunting. "9: There was fighting and destruction, especially Karasec," as written, though I think we'll see later Mr. McLeod interrupting there that it was Kozarac that he was mentioning. "... a suburb of Prijedor, and several people were captured. We have called them to free the women and children and let them go. They put the women and children in the front lines and followed with their weapons. The police and army accepted these women and children, and put them in buses and took them to safe havens. "In the course of the next few days, army and police captured several thousand people and put them into Trnopolje to protect them from the fighting with the extremists. That is how it was started as a collection centre." Can I pause there for a moment, Mr. McLeod. I know it's a long time ago, but can you remember was this all said, as it were, without interruption, a speech, rather than as the result of questioning?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that these were probably the opening remarks as an explanation which set the scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then he spoke about: "With the help of the ICRC, we've transported some of the inmates to -- " Clearly missed where he was saying, "but there are still some left, and we have evacuated those who want to leave this part of the country." Then he said: "We have also Muslims and Croatians in the camp who wish to remain, around 10.000. They have normal identification papers for our police. They are not accused of anything, and most of them are living in their homes but some are in the camp. A minority want to go to Croatia, and a majority want to go to Western Europe." And then he talked about contacts that they had had with UNHCR, the refugee arm of the UN, and said that there was a delegation coming to discuss the future of those who want to go to Europe. Then he said: "We have certainly heard about Omarska, where the people were caught with weapons, where 45 investigators interrogated the prison people. And as a result, 1.300 were transferred to the camp at Manjaca, and others either freed or transferred to the open camp here exclusively because their homes have been destroyed, so they have to go somewhere." Then he talked about the help of the local Red Cross and international help for food and medicine. And he welcomed the arrival of delegations and hoped that there would be more. And there was appeal for help to evacuate those who wanted to leave and gratitude expressed that there was a mission sent to Croatia because there were Serbs who had been there for a year. Then he was actually asked what specific help he wanted. Were the questions that you noted addressed to him by Sir John or by other people in the delegation, or a mixture?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think most of the questions came from Sir John. I think that -- I can't remember in this meeting, but certainly in some of the meetings, the other members of the delegation were also asking questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was asked about help he wanted with food and medicine. He said medicine first. Then he was asked what he thought about the long-term future. And he said: "I would like to say that we agree with the results of the London Conference. We see in these documents that have been accepted in London the possibility of ending the war. That makes us all suffer, and because I am the mayor of all citizens, of all citizens of Prijedor." He continued: "Neither Croatian nor Muslims left this territory, nor do we have the intention of kicking them out. There are some who hold appointments in the town and some are in the forces. "The future, however, is not clear because there is no electricity and the war is on. The communal government which has just met had on the agenda food and heating for the winter, and Mr. Kovacevic," as written, "is president of the regional government." And then apparently this gentleman intervened and talked about the problems with feeding and healing all the population, and the problems about electricity, fuel. And then he went on to say: "We are trying to solve our problems as we can, but trying to solve them for all the nationalities." Then there was more about electricity. And in paragraph 25: "The main problem is that the Muslims wage their war with electricity. The result is that no one has electricity, and CSCE can do something about it." And then it was said that the Muslims were waging their war with electricity. There were theories about food corridors, and a complaint that the Croats and Muslims were blockading or they should deblock Banja Luka airport. Then he was asked if the airport was used by the military, and he stated that it was a civilian airport; in wartime, used for military flights. And then Dr. Stakic intervened again and said: "There is equal treatment for all. Some Muslim areas have not been touched by war. We support your ideas about negotiations, and our representative, Mr. Karadzic, is ready to negotiate." And then he you got Mr."?", member of the regional government. Mr. McLeod, why is that? I mean, did you not hear his name or was a name not given?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: A name probably was given. I simply didn't get a note of it as the introductions were being made around the table, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you put "member of the regional government." How did you know that? Is that what was said?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that was my understanding of what his position was, and I was capturing a position even though I can't get a name. It's probably easier sometimes to understand somebody's title being described as opposed to actually getting a note of their name, as it goes around the table quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He intervened and said, "You said that you could not imagine these three peoples not living together. Was that in Bosnia, Herzegovina, or Yugoslavia?" And there was a reply of "Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then the man from the regional government said there was a lack of information and stated that Bosnia-Herzegovina is the same as Yugoslavia. Europe accepted Slovenia but does not look at 1.5 million Serbs in Bosnia. Europe has recognised Bosnia at the request of its president, who only represents 43 of the population. And went on to say that there was only a small part of -- I'm sorry, I better read this. "Europe should know that dealing with Bosnia-Herzegovina, that part of Bosnia is only a small part, and what happened in Yugoslavia happens here." Then: "The Serbs very probably accepted the cohabitation of three communities if it had not been for the declaration, the Islamic declaration, made on the formation of an Islamic state in 1986 and which was incorporated into the political programme." Had you heard about the so-called Islamic declaration before?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, it was something which was just part of the background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it went on to say: "The demographers had made projections that in less than 22 years, the Muslims will be a majority of over 50 per cent and the Serbs, who are the oldest people, have no wish to find themselves in the situation of a minority." And then there was a question or a comment that: "Although the Muslims already had a majority in the elections." And Mr Kovacevic went on. I think he just went back to prisoners. "We have a problem with the exchange of prisoners." And that there was an appeal that in talks with Mr. Izetbegovic the problems of exchange should be dealt with because the Muslim side will not accept exchange of prisoners. "Dr. Stakic: When we proposed the exchange of prisoners of war, we were told that these people were not Muslims. To get Serbs back, they asked for flour and guns, following the law of jihad." And then I think you were shown some Muslim currency but you couldn't take a photocopy because there was no electricity. Or what was said to be Muslim currency. And then the point was made that prisoner of war exchanges were important and they were asked if the people who were exchanged would be allowed back to their original villages. And the regional government gentleman, again, I take it, "Mr. ?" said that "A certain number of prisoners from the camp had been released who were from here and who are still around, but in proposing an exchange, we take a risk because we know, as soon as they go back, they will be mobilised and fight against us. We have already had experience of this." Then Dr. Stakic said: "Kozarac is still not yet a safe place because the extremists still come back and shoot. And yesterday, we had two casualties, and they were killed and set on fire. These groups have withdrawn to the mountain Kozara, and they come into town and do things. And even though we have soldiers and patrols, they cannot solve it. Experts in this sort of thing have come, and they say it could last 6 to 12 months. Hitler had 10.000 troops, and in four years, he did not get rid of the fighters there. "When we insist on not calling it a camp, it is because the Serbs from here know very well what a concentration camp is, particularly on the other side." And then there was the regional government man insisting on the idea of an exchange of prisoners of war because quite a few of them, when released, try to go to other countries. And there would be less people leaving Bosnia if there was an orderly exchange of prisoners of war. And at this point, the meeting was brought to a close and ended with Dr. Stakic saying: "We agree fully with what you said. We feel fully part of Europe. We are at a lower level, economically speaking, but we know we cannot enter Europe through war. We thank all the goodwill delegations who come here." I want to come back in a moment to your general impressions and conclusion. After you'd seen Dr. Stakic, did you go to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that the situation is this, that although you almost certainly wrote a report on what happened there, that has not actually been forwarded or we haven't acquired that. But did you give a description of what you found in Trnopolje in a letter to your father?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've copied just that part of the letter that relates to the description of Trnopolje. The rest, obviously, is a private letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But it's understood that their exists a report on Trnopolje provided by the witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, Your Honour, I should explain. We acquired the documents from ECMM themselves. They provided us with what documents they could find in their files, and it's from those documents that Mr. McLeod was seen, so it's the documents first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just recently, you said that "I think the situation was this, that you almost certainly wrote a report on what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. happened there. That has not actually been forwarded or we haven't acquired that." So there is a possibility to acquire this document. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Well, ECMM made a search of their files for us. They have not found that particular report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps Your Honours -- I don't think you have that yet because Mr. McLeod provided it last week. The Defence do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do object to it, Your Honour, if I may, and then give you the basis for the objection if the Court permits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, let us see whether we really have this letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You don't, Your Honours. I'm about to hand it up. Your Honour, if it helps my learned friends for the Defence, I'm not asking specifically that it be made an exhibit. It is more of a memory-refreshing document. It's not in the same category of an official report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably the compromise can be the witness may read out the part of his letter and then acknowledge that he had written this letter in the past. Then we have it on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We hand you a third copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, we have to hear the objections first of all of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, quite frankly, I think it's inappropriate for a witness who purports to be a professional who was sent on a specific mission to Bosnia, who wrote a report about the events that he experienced and saw in Bosnia, and who also kept what he considers detailed or otherwise copious notes of the meetings and his experiences in Bosnia, to have a letter be introduced that he wrote to his father in part. I think it's sufficient that this gentleman has actually prepared a written report, has provided us copies with his copious notes, and can testify based on his recollection of those items. It is in my opinion inappropriate to submit a letter, have the witness to read the letter, and then ask him if it refreshes his recollection. Perhaps this witness has an independent recollection, and until we exhaust that independent recollection, I do not believe it would be appropriate on the basis of law or fact to introduce this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you can better understand my line of questions on the report on Trnopolje. Evidently, if it's not available, this would be the best possible evidence. The second best evidence is, of course, the testimony of the witness before us. Therefore, we invited him. And no doubt, we may first of all ask him to tell us what he himself remembers, but then in addition, I would in a third step like him to read out that what he apparently has written at that time. I believe this is the correct order of introducing that what the witness can tell us. Would you please proceed in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, although it was ten years ago, I think you do retain a memory of what Trnopolje was like. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell Your Honours what you found when you went there.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. So this was a facility that at one point had been a school, and there were school buildings and then what presumably had been the playground or the playing fields bordered on two sides by a road. There were -- there was a sign hanging up in English and Serbian, saying the "open reception centre of Trnopolje." The facility was not surrounded by wire, unlike some of the other facilities that we saw. So it was clearly open. There were very large number of, I think, mostly men in the facility. Most of them seemed to have created for themselves shelters out of bits of plastic or boxes or whatever. The facility was characterised by the apex of the two roads, a machine post with a machine-gun pointing inwards rather than outwards, and we can debate what exactly it was there for. But there were certainly soldiers around the facility, their empty cartridge cases lying on the road at one place. So, obviously, there had been some shooting going on. When we got to the facility, we were able to go and talk to some of the inmates. On that occasion, they were free to come up to us, and so quite rapidly groups of them formed around us to try and find out what was happening, who we were. I was able to, because I speak German reasonably, to converse with some of them in German. I actually conducted an interview for one of the members of the CSCE rapporteur missions, who was a journalist, by translating her questions and getting the answers. And I think that interview appeared in Time afterwards, which was quite amusing, if you like. And fundamentally, the people that we were talking to were saying, "How long are we going to be here?" Because they wanted to know how soon they could get out. They explained the circumstances under which they had ended up in the camp, up to a point, and they said that there were some things they just didn't want to talk about, despite the fact that we were having a relatively private, public conversation. I suppose you could say the conditions there were extremely basic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that the machine-guns were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to get the -- you say there was a machine-gun post with a machine-gun pointing inwards rather than outwards. You say you can debate exactly what it was there for. You were told that this was a -- I think not a camp so much but as a place where people who had nowhere to go were going. What did the machine-gun post suggest to you as an army officer or ex-army officer?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The fact that there were armed men who were clearly in control of the facility and then a large number of unarmed men who were being held there, suggested that this was a facility where people were being kept. And while certainly they were free to move, to move around, I think that they were being kept there and didn't have a great deal of choice in the matter because there was nowhere else for them to go. And certainly, when we went back later on with the ICRC, they were quite happy to get on buses and then leave. So I think this was somewhere where they were being held pending whatever happened next.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then Your Honour, would Your Honour want him to actually read out what he wrote in his letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if you have been handed a copy yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I think, so that the Judges can hear you read your own letter, could you read it from the paragraph that begins, "I did another map reading job" down to the paragraph that ends: "The white flags on the roofs."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: "I did another map reading job to find our way to Trnopolje. And when we arrived, the first thing we saw were the machine-gun posts all pointing into the middle. We also found empty cases on the road. This was an open reception centre, and I took a photo of the sign in English and Serb. It was not clear how many people were in the camp, but guesses ranged from 1600 to 4.000. They all seemed to be men, and they were living in shelters that they had made out of plastic sheets. The most striking difference between Trnopolje and Manjaca was that, in Trnopolje, the men came up to us to find out what was going on. And once we started talking to them, large groups would form to listen. I wandered off first with the man from the health ministry, trying to get him to pose in front of one of the machine-gun posts. Then I wandered off with Lara, Robert Fisk's American wife, and translated an interview for her in German. It should have been in last week's Time, so a trip to the library is called for. The men I spoke to told a similar story to that of the mayor, with a few key differences of detail such as who had been shooting at whom. Once again, they wanted to know what was happening to them. And again, they said that the ICRC were keeping them alive. But they were things that even in this environment they refused to talk about. "We had been told by the mayor that there are also a number of Muslim villages where nothing had happened to the inhabitants. So Sir John asked to visit one. We drove back through Prijedor and around to the other side of the lake to a mixed Serb/Muslim village. The Muslim houses were identifiable by the white flags on the roofs."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. McLeod. Just going back to the paragraph where you translated an interview for Lara, Robert Fisk's American wife. Was Robert Fisk a journalist who was accompanying Sir John's mission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, during the drive back from Prijedor -- I'm sorry, to Prijedor, did you take some photographs of what you saw?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: On the drive back from Prijedor to Banja Luka, I took some photographs, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prijedor to Banja Luka. In addition to that, I think you've provided for us two photographs which we'll look at, taken at other times but during the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Your Honours have all got copies of those photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, I'd like you to have those photographs, and then we'll put them on the ELMO one by one and we'll just describe what they are. They should be in order. Photograph Number 1, is that a photograph taken at a place called -- this one I can't do --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Turnanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turnanj, which is near Karlovac, on the 23rd of July, 1992, showing people entering Croatian territory from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With an ECMM monitor, who we can see in the foreground of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But we don't lose control on the exhibit list, do you want to add these photographs to the S15?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, can I -- I think they ought to be separate and go with Mr. McLeod's exhibits. Could I ask that the report that he read out be made Exhibit S161.1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The report was not read out. You quoted in part from the report. Do you want to take this report --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The report of the meeting with Dr. Stakic. I read most of it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because on the transcript it reads "that he read out."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it was me. Could that be made S161.1. Sorry, I gather you haven't been doing points in this Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, S166 right now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the 92 bis materials which were admitted have been inserted, so now we jump to 166.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Your Honour, I'm in Your Honour's hands. I think the photographs ought to be kept together as a bunch of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's start -- first of all, objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at this time, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the report is admitted into evidence under Number S166A, and I understood it is available in B/C/S as well. This goes under S166B. In addition, we have an excerpt of a letter written by the witness, Mr. McLeod. Can you give us a detail: What do you think the date was you wrote this letter to your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It will be within a week of the event, so the -- at some point during the first week in September in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for clarification of this. This excerpt and the page you read out on this document, are they paragraphs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, is admitted into evidence as S167. And now we start the number of photographs, starting with S168. It should be included in the list of exhibits that the letter, S167, was read out and is therefore available in French and B/C/S. It was read out --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a B/C/S translation done because it was produced last Friday for the Brdjanin/Talic trial, so there is a B/C/S version of the letter as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is always better to work with Judges that are informed beforehand. We can find the translation at any rate of the French version on the transcript. So then we start with S168-1, that is the photo we have before us. Apparently, no 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. These photographs were not part of the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Then we continue in the order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Could we have the next photograph on the ELMO, please. They are in order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that shows -- that photograph was taken, was it, on the main road from Prijedor to Banja Luka travelling in the direction -- travelling east in the Kozarac area on the 31st of August?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The house that we can see standing in that photograph, what did you -- who did you understand that house belonged to, or what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I infer from the fact that the house appears to be still being lived in and is perfectly intact, that was probably a Serb house with a couple of Muslim houses next to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that become S168 -- 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. It is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: S167-2. 168-2. Thank you. And then the third photograph, please, could we have on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think same road and same date, 31st of August. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 168-3. The next photograph, number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see the -- I'm sorry, that it was taken on the same date on the same road. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know how closely you were able to examine these houses. Mr. McLeod, are you able to say was the destruction the result of apparently shelling or of some other means of destruction?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: By and large, this was something which was typical across all areas where there had been ethnic cleansing. It looked as if the houses had been burnt, which meant that the roofs would collapse as opposed to them being shot at or there being shell fire, in which case there would be quite different sorts of damage. So in some areas, you would see villages which had been clearly fought over, and others, villages that had been ethnically cleansed. And there you would start with having the roofs burnt off and then, in the most extreme cases, the entire house would be entirely flattened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then photograph, that was 168-4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The last two photographs, as there are no objections, are admitted into evidence as 168-3 and 4, and now it follows 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fifth photograph, please. Again, was that taken on the road Prijedor to Banja Luka, 31st of August?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the sixth photograph, please. That again on the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road, 31st of August?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the last photograph. That, I think, was taken on the 1st of October. And does that show the detainees being released from Trnopolje, accompanied by the ICRC and ECMM monitors actually walking through no-man's land between the Serb and Croatian front lines?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were there, Mr. McLeod. What was that walk like?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Basically very scary because it's a contact line which would normally be closed at dusk and have mines put across the road. We managed to persuade both parties to keep the road open and keep the mines just on the side of the road. So not the sort of thing you would normally want to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may those last photographs also be entered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. Therefore, the last photographs are admitted under S168-5 and -6.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Should be 7, I think, altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. The last one, -7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, finally, Mr. McLeod, I'd like to go back to that report you wrote of the meeting of the 31st of August with Dr. Stakic and look at your general impressions and conclusions, please. Paragraph 41, general impressions: "The version of the events that led to the opening of Trnopolje that we were given by the mayor was in stark contrast to that given by the people we spoke to in the camp." What was the stark contrast, Mr. McLeod, that you recall?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: One version of events was that the Muslim population had risen up and had somehow been attacking the Serbs by sending their women and children out first and then following on with their weapons. And as a result of the ensuing battle, the women and children had been put in one place and the men had then been captured and put into another place. The other version of events was that people had basically been rounded up in their houses, women and children had been taken off in one direction, and the men had been taken off in another direction. But the shooting had been started by the Serbs rather than the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it follows from that that the first version you gave was that of Dr. Stakic and the second version that of the people you talked to in the camp.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then your conclusion: "The authorities insist that they are acting in the best interests of all the people in their area and that they have no desire to get rid of the Muslim population. However, this just does not match what they are actually doing. Against this background, it is very hard to draw conclusions based on what is said. "The conclusion to be drawn from what we have seen is that the Muslim population is not wanted and is being systematically kicked out by whatever method is available." Now, Mr. McLeod, you wrote that after your visits to both Manjaca and Trnopolje and talking to the various politicians. Was that conclusion based on everything that you had seen and all the people you had spoken to, or just on your meeting with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that would then be the conclusion that I was making at the end of two days of meeting a number of politicians and seeing two camps and talking to people in two camps and, indeed, having experienced 9.000 people crossing over at Karlovac the month before. So this was a conclusion based on certainly more than just one conversation with one person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During the interrogation, you mentioned several times an article from the Time. Is it planned that the OTP tenders this document which was -- this was given indeed to us?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's not Time, Your Honour. That's another newspaper. We don't have the Time article. If we did, we can't find it. I think it's another article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, the problem that we receive documents with no date, no source, and nothing. But I can see it's a report by Robert Fisk and, therefore, I thought it could be this, just for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the reason I haven't put it in is because it's an article in a newspaper, and I'm having the witness here. It's not the article he referred to in Time magazine, it's an article by Robert Fisk, and I believe it comes from the Observer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Independent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The Independent, thank you very much. But the answer is no, I'm not putting it in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Then the trial stands adjourned until 10.40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May we then turn immediately to the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. McLeod.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my name is John Ostojic, and along with Branko Lukic, we represent Dr. Milomir Stakic. I'm going to ask you a series of questions here today. Although I read your reports and your testimony, I need some clarification on some points. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because we both speak the same language and in light of the fact that it is being translated in two other languages, at times you may note that I will pause, and I would ask you to pause before giving an answer and I'll try to do the same once you've given us an answer, before I proceed to the next question.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Guidelines.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Briefly, with respect to your background, sir, you told us that you left the British army. Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Why or -- why. I was working in Northern Ireland and decided that I would rather be doing something else than continuing in the army. And that was in part because I could see that the issues there were political rather than military, and therefore the way to solve the problem was to take a political course rather than a military course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you had a disagreement, in essence, with Britain's position on certain issues as it related to your duties at that time with Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it as strongly as that, but I could see that the answer was a political one rather than a military one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Focussing our attention here to this case and your mission in August of 1992, can you describe for me, prior to your mission, were you briefed or were you given any preparatory instructions or overview as to the situation in Bosnia, having just recently come from Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The ECMM had a briefing pack for new monitors. And I can't remember the exact detail that was in that, but that would certainly have covered the background situation as it then was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still have a copy of that packet that was provided to you during your briefing?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone provide you with an oral overview of the situation both in Bosnia and Croatia relating to your mission in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There was a daily briefing for all monitors in the headquarters and so, on a daily basis, the situation was being updated as far as we were aware, based on our teams around the whole of the former Yugoslavia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Still at the pre-mission stage, so prior to actually physically going to Bosnia, were you given an oral briefing of the situation in Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: As I said, on a daily basis, there was a briefing, and therefore the day before we went we would have had the most up-to-date briefing that was available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you will, what the goals of the mission were in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: So the aim of the ECMM or the aim of this particular mission with John Thompson?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The initial one, immediately when you started the first one in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Forgive me, sir. The mission of the ECMM as a whole? Or the -- because I was going into northern Bosnia in July, so hence my confusion. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's okay. You left the British military in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you decided to seek other employment, if you will, or different opportunities, if you will. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Different experiences. Right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From that moment on, when you left and became a member of the ECMM, can you tell me what were the goals that were outlined to you as being part of this mission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. So the basic aim of the ECMM was to attempt to put teams on to both sides of a contact line, to facilitate an understanding of the situation on both sides, and that understanding would be gathered by talking to the political or the military or, in some cases, religious leaders on both sides of a contact line, and then providing an impartial report back up to governments. And going beyond that, to enable the parties on both sides to have a dialogue to suggest a cease-fire and then to start confidence building measures with a two-fold view: Firstly, to provide an impartial report so that governments would know what was going on, and secondly, to try and bring the situation back to normality, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "both sides," sir, can you tell us who they were referring to when they told you "both sides"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: In each case, I'm referring to both sides of a particular contact line, and so on different occasions, the parties would be either -- any combination of the parties to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be any combination of the Croats, the Muslims, and the Serbs, depending on the contact line and depending particularly on the mission that you may have been on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So initially in June and July, the sides that you were trying to meet with, report on, and establish relationships with were whom?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: During the first part of my time with ECMM, I was working across both sides of the, if you like, internal contact line within Croatia between the Serb-controlled UNPA north and Karlovac, so Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Karlovac is?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. Karlovac is a town within Croatia southwest of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you created a report based on any of the interviews you may have conducted as it related in July of 1992 to -- regarding Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I would certainly have written reports on some of the missions that I was involved in during that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here, do you have a general recollection of your summary or impression relating to the mission that you took in Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you share that with us?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. This was a period immediately after a cease-fire had been arranged between the Serbs and the Croats in that part of Croatia. And the ECMM was involved in verifying that heavy weapons had been moved back from the contact line to storage areas. And one of our missions was to ensure that heavy weapons were, in fact, where they were supposed to be. Going beyond that, we were then also involved in very low level humanitarian activity, attempting to identify pockets of minority population on both sides and making sure that they were there in the first instance. People would say: "I believe that there is somebody living in this area. Can you go and find out?" So we would go and find out if there was still somebody there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to identify that mission in Karlovac as your first mission as a member of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think the very first mission I was doing was just straight down south from Zagreb, but fundamentally working in the Karlovac area was the first major piece of work that I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, that the impressions that you obtained from your experience in Karlovac left a long-lasting effect on you in terms of recollecting the events in Bosnia and Croatia in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly, some of them did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say -- strike that. Did the goals of the mission that you just outlined for us moments ago, did they change with respect to your visit in Banja Luka initially on August 20th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No. The aim was still exactly the same, but in order to carry out that mission, we first of all had to get the agreement of the Serbs that we could establish ourselves and operate on the territory that they controlled. So that was the very first step that we were engaged in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third mission, if I can identify it as such, was your return back to Banja Luka and your return to Bosanska Gradiska on August 30th, 1992. Correct? Those are separate and independent visits that you made?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yeah, that was the third time that I had been down into northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had the goal changed for this third visit from what it was in the first and second visits?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. On the third occasion, what we were doing was facilitating a mission by the CSCE rapporteur on the basis that we had the ability to take them into northern Bosnia and, therefore, we were providing, I suppose, a transport service for the rapporteur mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, isn't it true that your entire role with respect to this third mission was to provide transportation and to perhaps make some introductions, where necessary? Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was your goal at any time of any of the missions that we just talked about, was it to investigate?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: On every occasion, my aim was to try and capture my impressions and report, because one of the fundamental objectives of the ECMM was to provide impartial reporting for governments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you act in part as an investigator to determine what the true facts were relating to any particular issue?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that the term "investigator" which you're using is perhaps one that I would not have applied to myself. I was a monitor and, therefore, I was observing, as opposed to an investigator carrying out an investigation. I think there would be a subtle difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you share with me what you think your definition of an investigator is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think this is relevant. The witness said he regards himself as a monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you, sir, agree with me that no part of your goal or mission of any of the three missions that you had in July and August of 1992 was to assess blame to any of the parties, whether they be Croatian, Muslim, or Serbian? Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I would agree that I wasn't trying to apportion blame at all; I was simply trying to see what was going on. Where I detected that people were telling me lies, then I was trying to add as a comment that I thought what was being said was not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do any independent verification of any of the things that were said to you by the individuals that you purport you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Well, depending on exactly what your point is, then yes, because I met some people and then went and spoke to other people who were describing the same event. So yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To what extent did you conduct any independent verification or is that the extent of it as you've described it?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think you can see in my reports the full extent of the meetings I had and the people that I saw, and the comments based on what I saw at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me with this: Do you have any independent recollection of any of the conversations in which you were present with Dr. Stakic, or is it fair to say that the conversations are all reduced to the materials that you brought here with you today?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, it would be entirely fair to say that the -- apart from the fact that I can remember being at that place in the room, to get any sense of what he was saying, I would refer back, if necessary, to the handwritten note that I was taking as the interpreter was interpreting what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be also fair to say that Sir John Thompson accompanied you on this trip on August 30th, 1992, but had not accompanied you on the prior trip on August 20th, 1992. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's entirely accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On August 20th, we covered that you went to Banja Luka. From August 24th through the 29th, 1992, you returned to Zagreb. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then once again, on August 30th, 1992, you returned to Banja Luka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Essentially. And then according to -- at least, from my review of your testimony in prior matters as well as your report, you drove to Bosanska Gradiska, and you met the mayor there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you proceeded to drive south to Banja Luka, where you met the mayor there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And later that day, the day before you went to Prijedor, you went to Manjaca. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned to Banja Luka, and the next morning you drove to Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the meeting that you described for us, it was after that meeting that you proceeded to go to Trnopolje. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 31st, you returned to Zagreb, correct, 31st of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, how much time you spent in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I suppose we were there for about an hour or two for the meeting, and then I spent most of that afternoon on the edge of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing at the edge of the town? Was that visiting Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No. I had the unfortunate misfortune to end up with a flat tyre, and because we had Sir John with us, we had a satellite telephone with a generator, and the space where the spare tyre would normally have been kept in my vehicle had been taken up by the generator, so I didn't have a spare tyre. And so I guess the local police arranged for us to go to a Vulcaniser, the local term for a puncture repair shop, and they spent many hours fixing the tyre. It took them a lot longer than they thought it would because it was an armoured vehicle and the tyre was probably quite hard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, how much time was spent with the meeting in which you recorded or kept notes on where Dr. Stakic and others were present? How long did that meeting itself take?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Are you aware whether I wrote the time down on the... We started at 10.00. I'm not sure what time we finished, but it was probably an hour or hour and a half, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the witness, you're referring now to handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've gone back to my very original note that I wrote at the time, and I think that there is a typed version of this which is available. This is the very original.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've given it. There's a typescript of his original notes. And there's also, if Your Honours want it, a handwritten copy. I'm told you have that as well. If you can read it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We seem to get this day in, day out, Your Honour. These were given to Your Honour's assistant legal officer, somebody or other, Coralie Colson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Apparently, we haven't got it. If it's necessary for this clarification, for example, including the hours and times when this was taken. But I take it that it will --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, may I say it's not something that happens in both courts that I'm in. We hand up the documents in advance so that Your Honours have all these things. So we discover that Your Honours don't get them. So it's easy to hand them out in court. Your Honours, they are available, and we may have a copy of the notes here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: They are available for the Defence as well, these handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There seems to be a start time on the personal notes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me start the question again because my microphone was not on. There seems to be an indication of a starting time of the meeting, but no reflection as to how long the meeting lasted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that you have an independent recollection approximately ten years later that this meeting lasted an hour to an hour and-a-half?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It was not a very short meeting. There was quite a lot of discussion. So I would imagine an hour -- I mean, it's not a ten-minute meeting, it's not a four-hour meeting, but let's say an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your best recollection as you sit here ten years later. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the notes that you've kept and the report that you made September 3rd, 1992, as well as the letter that you shared with us with your father, you also gave a statement to the ICTY on or about March 16th, 2000. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I don't have a copy of the statement. But if that's when I made the statement, then yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately a year and a half ago, who was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Ms. Korner was there, and there was I think a French-Canadian investigator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't think so. I think it was the pair of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you asked by Ms. Korner any questions during your interview with her?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that we covered an awful lot of ground, and that was probably done by asking questions and giving answers, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a discussion between yourself and Ms. Korner and possibly the French-Canadian interviewer or investigator, I think you called him, as to whether you discussed the terms "Crisis Staff" or "war presidency"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think they may well have asked whether those were terms with which I was familiar. I think the answer would have been "I don't think so."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that what you recall?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yeah. With no record to go back to, and as a completely impromptu answer, yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do your notes at all reflect any mention with respect to the meeting of August 31st, 1992, "Crisis Staff" or "war presidency" anywhere?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There was a description of the... They called it "joint staff" or something. I don't think they called it a Crisis Staff, not that I have noted. But they certainly -- do you want me to try and find it, or do you know what the answer is?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I couldn't find it so -- but I don't want to give testimony here. If you'd like, I can, but no. It states here, sir, on page of your witness statement with the ERN number 00928879, and I'll read it: "I am familiar with the terms 'Crisis Staff' and/or 'war presidency,' but do not recall an exact example of their use by the Serbs whom I met at that time." Would that have been accurate, and is it still accurate today, sir, the statement that you gave on March of 2000?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It sounds as if my memory is quite good, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: So yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, in this statement, you described the conditions of the Trnopolje camp, and you described them in some detail, and you seemingly made a comparative analysis of the camp in Trnopolje and the camps that you visited prior, whether they be in Manjaca, Travnik, Zenica, or during your mission at Karlovac. Let me just make sure that I have this correct, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for Your Honours and for the Court and for my learned friend of the OTP, on page 3 of your March 2000 statement, you described Trnopolje as follows: "Trnopolje can be described more akin a refugee camp --" Let me start from the beginning. I tried to do it from memory and I failed. "Trnopolje can be described more akin a refugee camp than a prison because it was not surrounded by barbed wire, and the population was mixed by age and gender."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to that sentence, sir, what do you mean, "akin to a refugee camp"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: So, as I have described, it was another way perhaps to try and give the impression is of a shanty town that has been created out of plastic sheets and boxes and so on. The very stark contrast that was obvious that I have described is that Manjaca, for example, was a camp surrounded by wire, very regimented, obviously a military prison with a commandant who knew exactly what he was doing in terms of the Geneva Conventions. Trnopolje was an open piece of ground with a military presence around it and machine-gun posts, as I have described, but at that point, without a fence around it and without the same extremely strict discipline being imposed on the people being held at the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You proceed on page 4 of that statement you gave in March of 2000 to describe, on the first full paragraph: "People detained in the so-called "open reception centre of Trnopolje" were able to move freely within the camp." I want to ask you about that. Is that your accurate and correct recollection that the people within Trnopolje were able to move freely within the camp?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to go back to your prior thing, when you said it was a mixed age and gender, what do you mean when you say "mixed age and gender"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: What I was saying in the interview was that my impression was that there were men and women and children. Now, that conflicts with the letter I wrote almost immediately afterwards where I'd said it had been almost entirely men or entirely men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get do that in a moment or two. I don't know if it conflicts.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It is my opinion now, seeing the two things, or hearing you saying and seeing the other, there's a conflict there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it inaccurate that in March of 2000, when you described Trnopolje, you described it as a mixed facility, mixed of gender and age?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm quite clear that on subsequent missions when I went to Trnopolje, there were men and women and children there. Those were on occasions when the ICRC were removing people. And so I'm pretty clear about that. So it may well be that I had confused that visit with the very first visit. I'm sure that the letter I wrote at the time would be a more accurate reflection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it possible that when you wrote that in the letter to your father, you were actually describing Manjaca where, in fact, there were solely and exclusively men at that camp which you visited less than 12 hours prior to visiting Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No, there's no way I could have been confusing those two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to that letter in a second. Is it also true as you described that -- in your March 2000 statement, that the people there in essence were: "They were able to speak relatively openly with us"? Is that, sir, a fair recollection and assessment of that which you had with respect to the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "The facility was obviously under military jurisdiction." Is that also accurate and true today as it was in March of 2000, sir?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: As indeed it was at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: As indeed as it was at the time I was standing there, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go on to describe the guards. In the last sentence in that paragraph, you state: "The people were actually living in makeshift shelters." I think you described those makeshift shelters. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave your statement in March of 2000, did you have your notes and your report with you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I should think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about that Trnopolje was not surrounded by barbed wire. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here, do you recall whether it was or was not surrounded by barbed wire?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: At the time that I was there, there may have been some wire lying around, but it was not surrounded by a wire fence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're going to get to your report shortly. But finally, with respect to your March 2000 report, on page 4, the second full line which starts with "therefore," it reads as follows: "Therefore, in light of this, what I have been told by the inmates in Manjaca and what I had experienced in Karlovac on the 23rd of July, 1992, Trnopolje contained people who were in the process of being ethnically cleansed. This is what led me to make the conclusion that I drew in paragraph 42 and 43 of the report dated 03-09-92." My question to you, sir: Is it fair that if we are going to take Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your conclusions and impressions that appear on the report that Ms. Korner shared with us today, that because you rely on what you saw in Manjaca and what you experienced in Karlovac, that in order for us to get a deeper appreciation of those conclusions and impressions, we should look at your reports that you created for Manjaca and Karlovac? Correct?
