utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's your view. I have explained what I saw in Manjaca and Karlovac. I guess it's for the Court to decide what they want to know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that the report that you gave in connection with Manjaca is not relevant to your findings or impressions that you record following the end of your mission on August 31st, 1992, which you report about it on the September 3rd, 1992 memo that we discussed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that either you can take every single thing that I did and produce that as evidence or you can accept that I did various things and, as a result of those experiences, I drew some conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to your visit to the Manjaca camp and your meeting with the commandant, what was the date of that report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The report or the meeting?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Sir, that was the dated the 3rd of the 9th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same date as the report that you submitted here today as evidence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any other written reports that you made on or about September 3rd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There were two reports which I wrote about Manjaca, one describing the meeting with Colonel Popovic, one describing the camp itself. There was a report that I wrote about the meeting with Dr. Stakic; a report that I wrote about the meeting with Radic, who is the mayor of Banja Luka; and a report I wrote about the meeting with the mayor of Bosanska Gradiska. I think it's quite likely that I wrote a report about Trnopolje as well but I certainly didn't keep copies of any of these reports myself. I just have my notebooks, and nobody has been able to produce a copy of a Trnopolje report. So I assume I wrote one, but there isn't one here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have those reports from Manjaca and the meeting with the commandant of September 3rd, 1992, do you have those in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to those reports, would you agree with me that the first sections all relate to one another and, in fact, in the other two reports, you also reference Dr. Stakic? Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The preface to the report sets out that this was a visit which included meetings with a number of people, and to keep life simple, I was reporting each of the meetings as a separate document as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you also have a section for general points, which you shared with us, that this report should not be taken as a complete record of what was said. Do you remember that sentence in your report?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I was being very careful to say I didn't write down every single word that was said, but I tried to capture as much as I could as it was being interpreted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I direct your attention to paragraph 3 of your report dated September 3rd, 1992. Are we there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The third section which says "general points," would that generally be like a waiver of some kind that you give or a caveat of some sort, or what is the purpose of that paragraph or those paragraphs in section 3?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel and witnesses please make pauses between question and answer, thank you, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You don't have the headphones on. Please avoid overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was simply making clear that the report should not be taken as a complete verbatim record of the meeting in such a way that the transcript of this trial is a complete verbatim record. I was saying here is something which I have produced which reflects most of what was said or, indeed, some of what was said, and is my best effort but is not a perfect record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You proceed on page 1 of that report, paragraph 5, to discuss or take notes regarding the introductory remarks made by Dr. Stakic. And he discussed with you the shameful murders of the army of Bosanska Krajina and the police. Do you see that in the last sentence of your report on page 1?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you, sir, at any time briefed or advised of the situation which led to the events in the Prijedor Municipality, such as, were you advised by anyone that, in fact, on May 2nd, 1992, a police officer was killed?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I don't think that we had been through a detailed chronology of every single event that had taken place. I think that my colleagues who were with me who had been working in Banja Luka up to that point would probably have had a far better recollection than me of the events leading up to the point when they had certainly left. I think it would then be fair to say that there was a gap in our knowledge of precisely what was going on between then and when we returned as a mission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point, sir, did you know what, if anything, Dr. Stakic was referring to, according to your notes, when he discussed the murders of the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any time from your colleagues ask to know what references Dr. Stakic was making in connection with these murders?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time, sir, learn from any of your colleagues that in fact there was an incident at a checkpoint in Hambarine on May 22nd, 1992, wherein, depending on whose view, one or more soldiers were killed and injured?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told, sir, at any time by any of your colleagues or informed by others that on or about May 24th, 1992, there was an attack on a military convoy that was proceeding through the area of Kozarac from Banja Luka towards Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention, sir, to paragraph 15 of your report, which is on the second page. Before we touch upon that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. As you know, we always try to follow what you are saying. And I have paragraph 15 on the page 3. Probably you're discussing a separate document because we have two reports on Manjaca available. You are discussing the one concluding with paragraph 16?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm referring to his third report of September 3rd, 1992, which is the detailed report in which Mr. McLeod discusses -- relates the discussions that were had between Dr. Stakic, among others. And it is within that report only, I believe, that Dr. Stakic referenced or -- according to Mr. McLeod, referenced the shameful murders of the army in the first page of that report, paragraph number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, according to your notes, I think on the last page of that note, would it be fair to describe that the individuals that you met were actually genuine?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The very final comment that I wrote, and here I was talking about specifically the policeman who had been escorting me out who were very fed up to have had me overstaying my welcome somewhat because of the flat tyre, so that -- I think it was as they handed over escorts that prompted me to write that comment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to look at that note that you made and can you share with us if you say "the individual who escorted us" or "the individual who helped me repair the flat on my tyre" or do you say, in fact, "all individuals that we met are indeed genuine"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: All right. Well, the -- I don't know if you can see that. So it's almost illegible in my original handwriting, but that says: "As individuals, all these guys are quite genuine."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you share with me who you were referring to when you made that comment or statement in your notes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think I was prompted to write that because we had just swapped over police escorts, and they were being quite genuine in their attempts to look after me, get rid of me as fast as they could. I had spent the afternoon with a bunch of people working extremely hard trying to fix a very difficult flat tyre. Going beyond that, I think it's fair to say that most of the people whom I met in the former Yugoslavia, as individuals, appeared to be doing their best to do whatever it was that they were doing. What I found very ironic was that sometimes what they were doing struck me as being quite barbaric or wrong, but didn't seem to strike them as such. And I think that characterisation would be fair across most of the parties across most of the former Yugoslavia where I was operating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the notes that you have, you reference -- according to the typed script that we have, you identify an individual as "boss," b-o-s-s. What does that mean? It's on page 53, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that's probably John Thompson. It's certainly somebody on our side of the table as opposed to the other side of the table, I think, looking at the context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the context of your notes and you compare it with your summary of September 3rd, 1992, as to who spoke when, am I wrong that really you were referring to someone that you identify in paragraph number 29?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. Well, in that case, since I wrote this report immediately afterwards, I probably had a better recollection at that stage of who was saying what. And therefore, I would imagine that was a senior member on the other side of the table making a comment in response to something that we had been saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the notes that you took were actually taken contemporaneous with the actual discussions that were being had, whereas your report was three days later. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So just so that I'm clear, does "boss" mean the person who you identify in that paragraph number 29: "Mr. ?, member of the regional government"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that must be the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does it mean to you when you wrote down "boss"? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Somebody who had been identified as a senior member of the team, and it wasn't particularly easy to catch everybody's names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to paragraph 15 on page 2 of your report, if I may, do you recall those words that you state or attribute to Dr. Stakic having been given by Dr. Stakic, or are you solely and exclusively relying on the notes that you have in connection with the discussion of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I would entirely rely on this, and I'm fairly certain that the initial exposition was given by him, and thereafter it broke down. And I was attempting to pick up who the individuals were who were then making other points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You identify that you went to see the mayor of Prijedor, and you subsequently identified that person as being Dr. Stakic. Did you find it odd at that time that here he was a mayor of a town, Prijedor, and he's, in fact, telling you, as you recorded in your notes and as you recorded three days later, September 3rd, 1992, that he would have told you, "We have certainly heard about Omarska," et cetera. Did that strike you as being odd that he had "heard" about it? Or was he being genuine and forthright at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I honestly can't remember what my thought was at the time. Sitting here, it would strike me as being very odd, given that Omarska is just down the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time, sir, did Dr. Stakic tell you that he knew or that he set up Omarska or was involved in any way with Omarska?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time, sir, did Dr. Stakic ever tell you that he played any role at all in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only thing that you record in your notes is, in fact, that Dr. Stakic sharing with you that they heard about Omarska. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You proceed on page 3, among other things, to have another discussion with Dr. Stakic, and paragraph 20 is what I'd like to direct your attention to, if I may. You quote essentially, or you paraphrase, Dr. Stakic as saying he was in agreement with the London Conference, in essence. Did you prior to your mission have an understanding and appreciation of what the negotiations were, both the content and the results, of the London Conference?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm sure that at that time I would have been aware of the results. Right now, if you ask me to be precise, I can't remember exactly what the outcome was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find it a good thing, a positive thing, or a negative thing that Dr. Stakic would have agreed with the results of the London Conference?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I simply can't remember, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on that paragraph, number 20, and according to your notes, would it seem that Dr. Stakic was a proponent of war, or would you be left with the impression that he was one of the people who wanted the war to end?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that he would have wanted -- this is based on a slightly broader context than just this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this paragraph, after that which you've heard.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: He was saying he wanted the war to end, and he was saying that he would have been pleased with my recollection of the result, which would have been that there would be a Serb canton. And part of the process that was going on was to make sure that that would have been a Serb canton with only Serbs living in it. That's not exactly what he was saying, but that is what -- that is what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, it was quite the opposite of what he was saying if he wanted the Serb canton, did you even write in your report: Here's a gentleman who says he -- or I think he wants a Serb canton on one hand, and on the other hand, he's telling me that he's the mayor of all the citizens of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that you'll find that's the conclusion of my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the conclusion of your report as you described on March 2000, which includes the impressions that you arrived and the impressions that you were left with from meetings of mayors of different municipalities, including Bosanska Gradiska, including your visit in Manjaca, including your visit in Karlovac on July of 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Was that impression that you claim you made on September 3rd, 1992, solely as it relates to Dr. Stakic, or did it also include the other individual mayors that you met, the other military men that you met in Banja Luka and in the other municipalities that you visited?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It was the impression that I had formed both about what Dr. Stakic was saying and indeed all the people putting across the Serb point of view were saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a general categorisation, correct? The reason I'm asking you is this, sir, and let's just put it out there: In the other reports, I notice that you don't reach that conclusion. Would I correct, if we only took your report from Manjaca, that as it relates to the people that you met in Manjaca, you didn't reach that conclusion? Would I also be correct, sir, that as it relates to the meetings that you had in Banja Luka, the meetings that you had at Karlovac, the meeting that you had at Bosanska Gradiska, that you did not, since you didn't include it in your report, have that impression of those people?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that by the time that I had finished that two days there, then I would have applied that impression to all of them. Certainly, I had a better view having been inside Manjaca and inside Trnopolje, which is why I think chronologically I would end up reaching that conclusion at the end of the period of writing the reports in chronological order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's a rather broad statement that you made, you were painting, for lack of a better phrase, with a rather broad brush at that time; correct? I mean, you're generalising, making broad statements? You're not specifying to whom, if anyone, that comment relates to, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No, I think that I am saying quite precisely here that what I had heard Mr. Stakic saying -- Dr. Stakic saying - I apologise - was completely at odds with what I was seeing. And I was evidencing the conclusion that I was reaching about it being at odds with the fact that I had seen several other things going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to paragraph 37 of your report on page 5, please. I just want to clarify a point that was read into the record by my learned friend, Ms. Korner. Are you there? Sorry. With respect to that, did you have any background information as to what the comments were relating to when Dr. Stakic having been attributed to saying that "Hitler had 10.000 troops and in four years he could not get rid of the fighters there"? Did you know in essence what Dr. Stakic was referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure at what level of detail you want to go to, but yes, fundamentally, there had been an occupation of Yugoslavia by the Germans and there had been a very strong resistance, and I think he was referring to the resistance probably put up by the Serbs in that part of the world against the Germans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Otherwise known as the Partisans, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In essence, he was trying to describe to you that the terrain that was there, namely, in the Kozara area, was already battle tested and it was impossible, according to his view, to -- in essence, either capture, arrest, or detain all the people because that area has been historically well known as an area that even Hitler's 10.000 troops could not clean out. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many people in Trnopolje did you speak with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: At least two or three individuals and then they -- as members of quite large groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your general impressions section, paragraph 41, you state: "The version of the events that led to the opening of Trnopolje that we were given by the mayor was in stark contrast to that given by the people we spoke to in the camp." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people you're referring to there were the two or three people that you just mentioned. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I spoke to two or three people. I think other members of the team also spoke to people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are you referring to in your comment, note, under paragraph 41, "general impression"? Is it your general impression, the group's general impression, or someone else's general impression?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly the impression that I got based on the people that I spoke to leads to this conclusion. I think that I was not alone in reaching that conclusion amongst the other members of the group, but you would have to invite other members of the group to come here and explain to corroborate what I think is -- was their view at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You write a letter to your father shortly thereafter in September of 1992, but you share with him quite a different view as to whether or not there was a stark contrast between what the mayor told you and what the people told you. In fact, in the letter to your father, you state as follows: "The men I spoke to told a similar story to that of the mayor, with a few key differences of detail such as who had been shooting at whom." Can you reconcile that for me, sir? Was it in stark contrast or was it as you told your father, that it was a similar story, that the people shared the similar story? How do you think it's funny?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It most definitely is not a funny subject at all, sir. The issue is your play with words, I think. Allow me to explain. So what you have is a version of events which says the Muslims started shooting at us, they sent the women and children out in front. We had to take the women and children away in buses for their own safety. And then we captured the men and put them into camps, again, largely for their own safety and because they have nowhere to go --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Nowhere in your report does it say that Dr. Stakic said, "We captured the men." It says that the military and the police captured the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Stop. Can we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I just wanted to interrupt everybody pressing the priority button. We can't proceed this way. You asked a very, very difficult question, and then you have to give the witness a chance to answer in the full context. He has to explain to the Judges what he wants to say and not to stop where you don't want him. Please. Please continue with the answer. You answered a sentence: "Again, largely for their own safety and because they have nowhere to go." And then the transcript stops, unfortunately. Please proceed with your entire answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, to keep it very simple, you have one version of events which starts with armed Muslim men pushing the women and children in front of them into the arms of the Serbian forces, who take the women and children in buses to somewhere for their safety and then take the armed men somewhere else for their safety, as a very condensed form of one version of events. And the other version of events is very similar because the -- what happens to the women and children is exactly the same. They are separated from the men and they are taken away. And the men are then certainly taken away and put into camps. And I have seen the men in the camps. But the difference is that in this version, the Serbs have come and taken the women and children away, and then taken the men and put them into first one camp and then another camp. And the similarity is that the same events are being reported. The stark difference is that. According to one side -- each side is saying that the other side started it. So that is the stark difference that I refer to. I hope that that's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you started giving your answer, Mr. McLeod, you said that I'm trying to play with words or something to that effect. But in fact, you're the one who used the exact same words "stark contrast" in both your September 3rd, 1992 -- or in your 1992 letter. Correct? Those aren't my words. And you're the person who wrote in the letter that you gave to your father that it was "the men" told you a "similar story to that of what the mayor told you." So sir, respectfully, those aren't my words. Those are your words. And I'm merely just trying to seek clarification on that. So it's not a play on words. They are not my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. words.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. So one last time so we're quite clear, there is a stark contrast between the two explanations that are given for how the events took place. Events as they are described are broadly similar. But what struck me was that there was a diametrically opposed explanation for the similar events as they are described, and it struck me that the version of events given by the Serbs was simply not credible, based on the events that I could see with my own eyes at the time. I hope that that's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 42 of your conclusions the last sentence, it states: "Against this background, it is very hard to draw conclusions based on what is said." Can you tell me, sir, what do you mean "against this background"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Against the background of a number of people who were saying: "We want to have a multi-ethnic community and we want to be responsible for all parties within this community, and we want to be members of Western Europe and, indeed, we want to be democratic." So these are the statements which have been made by a number of people that I have met by then, including Dr. Stakic, some of them. So they are saying one thing, and what I'm actually seeing on the ground suggests something which is different to that, so that's the background that I'm alluding to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say these other statements which have been made by a number of people. Are you including in that the people during your visits on August 20th and August 30th, 1992, namely, the mayors of these other towns or municipalities as well as the military men you may have interviewed or had discussions with?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was against that entire background as a whole, as opposed to based on solely the meeting that you had on August 31st, 1992, in Prijedor. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Stakic was simply expounding the same view that I had already heard on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an issue, if you recall, during your visits with the people in the Banja Luka and Prijedor area regarding how the Muslims were waging war, in essence, if I can just direct you to it, an issue of electricity and electrical power being cut off. Do you remember that discussion?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it, sir, that there was hydroelectric generating plants in central Bosnia at the time that were controlled by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It's my understanding, as opposed to technical precise knowledge, that before the war there had been hydroelectric power which had provided power for large parts of Bosnia, and those were in central Bosnia, and the transmission lines between there and northern Bosnia had been cut. Now, in practice, I don't know whether the hydroelectric plants were still working anyway, but there was no power getting through.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, in your notes in trying to prepare an accurate and concise rendition of the facts that you experienced, did you, sir, record anywhere these conversations that you had with members or the people who were detained in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I didn't write a note at the time, and I think what I captured later on was in my reports and indeed my letters, my recollection of what they had said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a note here that on page 20 of today's transcript, line 17 through 20, and I ask the registrar and counsel and, obviously, the Court just to double check this, that in connection with your testimony involving the men that you spoke with in Trnopolje, you state: "The men I spoke to told a similar story to that of the mayor." Or thereabouts. I shouldn't maybe put quotes on it. My question to you, sir: What was the similar story that the men who were being detained at Trnopolje, that they were sharing with you, that was similar to what you heard from Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: As we have just been through it at some length, they were describing the series of events which led to them being in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, as you sit here, or maybe even in -- you're welcome to look at your notes. Who all was present at the meeting on August 31st, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: With Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, somebody to write his name down for me, a number of gentleman who were politicians. Shall I go through the notes and identify the ones that I have? That would probably be --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First tell me if there were more people present than those who were reflected in your notes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many in total?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I remember that the room was very full, so you probably have about 16 or 20 people down two sides of a table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many were from the delegation that you were involved in, how many members of those 16 to 20?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'd say -- I seem to remember we had more or less equal numbers on both sides of the table. It was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Eight to ten on each side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It would be a reasonable guess at this stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the Court would be kind enough to instruct the usher to place the pictures on the ELMO, specifically S168-2, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I may see the pictures and then I can correct it. Just those two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel please be so kind and take into account that we have to make a break at 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm hoping to conclude with Mr. McLeod before the -- I thought we were ending today at 12.45, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We proceed as long as justice requires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to the photograph that we see on the ELMO, can you tell us, sir, the date of that photograph?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that's the 23rd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was actually leaving Prijedor and going into Croatia, as I think in general was your testimony in describing this photograph? Do you know what the ethnic background of those persons or people were?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I believe the majority of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, just for the record, the identification number of that picture so that, when we review this later, we won't be confused with other pictures. Is there an indication on the back side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: S168-1. Thank you. With respect to that, sir, are you familiar with the licence plate that appears on that picture, and is it true that the PD on that licence plate is actually a licence plate from the municipality of Prijedor? Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Well, I can see that the licence plate has a "PD." I'm not familiar with that being a Prijedor licence plate, but I accept that it might be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with what the licence plate was for vehicles that were owned by any of the citizens in Prijedor at or about June or July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have the next picture, please, placed on the ELMO. If you take a look at that picture, sir, it seems to me, but correct me if I am wrong, that there are some wood partitions that are seen on some of the homes that were obviously destroyed. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Forgive me, I'm not quite sure what you mean by wood partitions, that this structure appears to be wooden?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are some portions within that structure that are wooden. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You earlier testified that the homes, or some of the homes that you took pictures of, seem to have been burned down or sustained some level of fire. Can you describe for me whether you think that the fire caused the hole on the side wall of that building and the fact that, at least on this picture, there is little, if any, evidence of any burn marks. Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I would suggest that that building has been blown up rather than burnt, although as we see in some of the other buildings quite clearly have smoke damage on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it fair to say, sir, that you don't know when those buildings sustained the smoke damage? You didn't see it happen, correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of all the pictures that you have, can you tell me whether any of the pictures were from areas in the Prijedor municipality other than the area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: They were all taken as a series just driving down that one road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was down one road, in one town, and it didn't include any other roads or any of the other towns such as Puharska or any of the buildings or homes that were on or around the area of the town of Prijedor itself. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, but we have to make the necessary break. Now the trial stands adjourned until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, a couple questions just for clarification. Earlier we had discussed -- I think you made a comment during an exchange that we had that Dr. Stakic said, "We captured several thousand people." With respect to the "we," isn't it true, sir, that your notes, specifically on the first page, when it discusses "in the course of the next few days," page 50 of the typewritten notes -- are you there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm on page 50, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to who captured several thousand people, I think your comment during some of the cross was that you used the word "we," if I'm not mistaken. Just to clear that up, in your notes that you have in front of you, as well as the typewritten version, in fact, Dr. Stakic never says, "We captured several thousand people." He indeed states the army and police captured them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also on your September 3rd, 1992 report, specifically paragraph 11 of that report, again discussing the issue of who captured whom, a note attributed to Dr. Stakic, he again identifies the people who captured, that would be the army, and as you have it here, the police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether you and Sir Thompson at any time actually drove around Prijedor to see other homes inhabited by Muslims which were not either destroyed by a result of shelling or, as you have stated, being burned down?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where are those pictures?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I don't think that I took a photograph of those houses. Other members of the team certainly did and so it ought to be possible to find pictures, but I certainly don't have any with me now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'd like to know is that you discussed or you agreed that the pictures you shared with us today were from this one road in Kozarac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at your letter that you wrote to your father, you in fact describe the situation wherein and Sir John, I think it's Sir John Thompson, correct? Yes, that you reference?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you were invited to see the homes of Muslim inhabitants in the mixed villages. In your letter to your father, nowhere do you state that, in fact, those homes in other areas that we viewed were or were not destroyed, burned, or shelled. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: In the page of the letter that we have here, I don't say that. I can't remember what else is in the letter. Again, we could go and find the original letter, but I don't propose to do that right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. And I only have the page that was summarised for me. So based on that, at the very least, that which purports to be the only items in your letter wherein you discuss your journey to Bosnia during that period?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think, as you can see, it's quite a long letter, and I sat down, and as part of my way of trying to deal with what I had seen was just writing down what I had seen and done. I'm fairly sure that I would have described the other village, but I don't have the letter here, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who has a copy of that letter, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I don't know if my father still has a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Presumably, he would have the original, and you would have retained the copy. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all the questions we have, Your Honour, of Mr. McLeod. We would like, though, the record to reflect and we're asking at this time that the reports from the meetings as this witness has stated, we believe, in cross-examination the reports that relate to the general impressions and comments section of his report, namely, the Manjaca meeting with commander as well as the description and a view of the Manjaca camp that Mr. McLeod has, in a separate report, identified. We recognise that Manjaca is not part of this case or this indictment, but we believe that it's relevant in order to keep those general impressions and comments in a context in which the Court and all of us can appreciate. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do I understand that the Defence tenders the documents on the mission to Banja Luka, the meeting with commandant of prisoner of war camp Manjaca dated 3 September, 1992 into evidence? You want to tender this, or you want to tender both?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In addition, the report that's identified from September 1st, 1992, which is a meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, not to confuse. We have two reports on Manjaca, both dated 3 September, 1992. You want to have them both admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please help out. It's D12, or already 13?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D14, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the report of 3rd of September, 1992, registration number 00950310, is admitted into evidence under D14. The one from the same date with the number 00950308 is admitted into evidence under D15. What about the other reports the Defence touched upon, first of all, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would like that report as well dated September 1st, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's start in the order of the appearances. The first one is the one from 20 August, 1992, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, the report from the Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I ask you, do you want to tender this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to come back to this. The next one, Banja Luka, second visit, 25 August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you please make me understand why you want to have the second visit but not the first visit?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, because I believe the witness specifically stated that it was his visit and journey from the third trip, which is one that he made in the Prijedor area. So I, quite frankly, perhaps misunderstood the Court. There's a specific report that he made relating to the meeting with the mayor of Banja Luka on August 30th and 31st, and it was that meeting and that memo that I was looking at. I think for relevance purposes, based on Mr. McLeod's testimony, at least from our purposes, we would like those meetings vis-a-vis the Banja Luka meeting, Bosanska Gradiska meeting, the Prijedor meeting and the Manjaca meeting, be kept in the context in which I believe the witness testified, because that was a two-day trip. So it's those reports that I would like to be submitted in as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have to come back to this later then. Now you're referring to the number 00950336, meeting with the mayor of Bosanska Gradiska, being also in the context of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. That is the correct minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And this document with the 00950336, if there are no objections by the OTP. I can see none. Therefore, admitted into evidence as D16. And the next one, meeting with the mayor of Banja Luka, 1st September, 1992, document 00950347, the first page?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I can see no objections. Admitted into evidence as D17. Thank you. This concludes the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the OTP, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No re-examination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, may I ask you several questions in addition. It starts with a really tiny detail. On page 4 of your report, you said: "At this point, we were shown what was claimed to be Muslim currency. We were unable to take a photocopy because there was no electricity. However, I asked for one." First point: Is it true that during the entire meeting, it was relatively dark in the room, or was there electricity? Was it possible to make photographs in the room, and to come to the point, were there made photographs in this room?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: The room was bright, lots of daylight. I don't remember whether anybody took a photograph in the room. I certainly did not. And I can't remember whether there were lights on. I think it was just daylight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. But you, yourself, you have no photos available from this meeting. To stay with this really minor detail, you asked for -- as a photocopy or that what was shown to you, Muslim currency. What do we have to understand this term and what was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: They produced a note of currency, so a paper note. They said this is a piece of Muslim currency. It proves that they are trying to establish their own state by having currency as one of the things which a state produces, and this was being produced as evidence that the Muslims were trying to form their own state within Bosnia. And, therefore, we were interested and said, "Can we please have a copy or even an original?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you get?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You said "they." Could you please, before answering, have a look on your handwritten document, coming to this point, and then try to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Could you help me to find the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is called "comment" immediately after number 35.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Okay, looking at the order in which the text comes, I would imagine, because the person who is speaking immediately before I made that note was Dr. Stakic, it was probably Dr. Stakic who then produced it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you have no recollection now that you could say Person A, Person B, or Person C showed me this, as you call it, Muslim currency note?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I couldn't say specifically which person it was. It was certainly somebody on the Serbian side who said, as proof of his point, "Here is their currency."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You were already asked beforehand how many persons were present at this meeting. You came to the meeting. There was an opening speech and some remarks of introductions were made. Who approached first and whom -- these are two different questions. Who spoke first from the other side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm fairly certain it was Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: According to the document, this seems to be correct. And the second question is, after -- following your impression, who was the one who had -- or if several, please, tell us. Who was the one having the say on the other side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: There were a number of people who were making comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Was there --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: A hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A kind of hierarchy, you had the impression?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think, within the government, the most senior person there was a gentleman from Pale, I understand from the health ministry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The one you quoted as a person wearing a pistol and having a machine pistol in his car. Right?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which evidently was surprising for you as a representative of the Ministry of Health.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. And then?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: And then there was clearly -- I inferred that there was then a regional government, and then there was the Prijedor opstina. And so Dr. Stakic was -- he was a civilian representative running Prijedor. And then there was a layer above him and then a layer above that from Pale, I think would be my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And during this discussion held the 3rd of September, 1992, who was among the persons on the other side, if we speak in these terms? The side of the monitors and on the other side, the representatives of Prijedor, who was after -- following your impression, the most important person on the other side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: To be quite correct, sir, the meeting was on the 31st of August, not the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The report.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Having different levels of control, the gentleman from Pale had previously said that he had it within his ability to write an order authorising the closure of all the camps, so he obviously had some jurisdiction, or he appeared to have some jurisdiction there. Within Prijedor, I think that Dr. Stakic was probably the person who was, along with the military and the police, controlling matters in that opstina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned in your report Dr. Stakic, Mr. -- as it's shown in the report, a Mr. Kovacic. May it be that this person has the name "Kovacevic," that there was an error committed on your -- on the basis of your perception of the names you got as you got them?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was ever an attempt made to find out who was the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. third person, this "Mr. ?," as we can see it from the document?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that other members of the team may have had a better record than I did of who was sitting around the table. In my case, I was able to -- I will show you. As Dr. Stakic started to talk, I asked - I think it was a gentleman from Pale sitting next to me or certainly somebody who was sitting next to me - to identify who he was, and so they wrote it out for me. And as you can see, they wrote it out first in the Cyrillic script which I can't understand, which is why it was then translated back into ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was not done with this, sorry to put it this way, as we can read it, "Mr. ?"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In paragraph 28 of your statement, you state: "We support your ideas about negotiations and our representative, Mr. Karadzic, is ready to negotiate." Is there any doubt that Dr. Stakic called Mr. Karadzic as "our representative"? It was 28.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I see the reference in my report, sir. I was wondering if it was worth going back to the original note, but I'm fairly sure that I simply copied from the original into this. I'll go back to the original if you would like me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please. It's slightly before the other portion we just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what I wrote. So that is what the interpreter would have said as her translation or his translation, his translation of what was being said. So if we accept that it has been through an interpreter, then that is the note that I wrote at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, have it still before you because I want to come to one page later, paragraph 37. There Dr. Stakic is quoted as having said: "Kozarac is still not yet a safe place because the extremists still come back and shoot. And yesterday, we had two casualties and they were killed and set on fire." Also, once again with the reservation that it has gone through interpretation only, the word "extremist" was used?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From your own recollection, could you tell us what was meant or who was meant by "extremist"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think he was referring to Muslim extremists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Going a few lines ahead under 38: "When we insist on not calling it a camp, it is because the Serbs from here know very well what a concentration camp is, particularly on the other side." No doubt that this was said by Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Following once again your recollection, what is the meaning of what a concentration camp is, particularly on the other side? What's the meaning here of "on the other side"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think he could have been referring to either one of two things, sir, either the fact that Serbs had been held in concentration camps during the Second World War, which would have fitted into the context, and then referring to "on the other side," I think he was referring to the fact that a large number of Serbs were being held by the Croats and the Muslims in central Bosnia. So "on the other side" meant on the other side of the internal contact line within Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Coming back to paragraph 21, it was said, "Neither Croatian nor Muslims left this territory, nor do we have the intention of kicking them out." Once again following your notes, is this the correct quotation, and why just mentioning Croatian and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: What I have written here is: "Neither Croatians or Muslims left this territory, nor do we have the intention -- "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Neither Croatians or Muslim, yes?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Why this specific mentioning "Croatian or Muslims"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I would assume that there had been a mixed population with some Croats living in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was there any dissent amongst the persons giving statements from the other side?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: In terms of them disagreeing with the statements they were making?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So one could, in general, attribute also the comments made by Mr. Kovacevic and the other person, the third person, "Mr. ?," to Dr. Stakic? Dr. Stakic never opposed to what was said by the two other persons you mentioned in your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me now turn to your visit to Manjaca. You prepared two reports, and one is -- stops, the second one admitted into evidence, under paragraph 16, under the heading "reaction of the authorities: The commandant Colonel Popovic was very clear that he wanted us to see everything and report accurately. However, we were not allowed to see everything, and some questions were ignored. He quoted the Geneva Convention to justify all his actions. A separate report is being written on his interpretation of the Geneva Convention." Here it's not necessary to come back to this point because this is attributed to Colonel Popovic, but my point is, was -- in relation to the situation in Prijedor, or possibly Trnopolje, was ever the question raised whether or not the responsible persons obeyed the rules of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I don't think so, and I think that was because people did not consider in the main that these were prisoners of war in the same way that they were considered to be prisoners of war at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So could you -- I know you touched upon this issue slightly. Could you give us, please, your view on the distinction between these two camps?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: From the point of view of what their function was as far as the Serbs were concerned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that there was basically very little difference because both of them were places where they were holding Muslim men predominantly, entirely in Manjaca, and predominantly in Trnopolje at that point. I don't know whether they were under different jurisdictions from a control point of view, but both of them appeared to have military people actually running the camps. I think Colonel Popovic was running his camp in a different way to the way that Trnopolje was being managed, but the function was exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you remember who was the commander of Trnopolje? Did you speak with or to him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm sure that when we arrived, we had an explanation from somebody, probably the commander. I don't have a note of his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was Trnopolje - the Defence asked already in part this question - or Keraterm or Omarska ever mentioned during the discussions with Dr. Stakic and others?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I apologise, I don't quite understand the question. So Dr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During the discussions with Dr. Stakic, Mr. Kovacevic and the third person, was it ever discussed what is the purpose of, say, Trnopolje camp, who is responsible for this? And the same question would be true as regards Keraterm and Omarska.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think in terms of Omarska, my note says that he was aware of it. He had heard of it. I think in terms of Trnopolje, he certainly knew all about it because we were going there next and this was facilitated by the people that we were meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you go to this point a little bit more in detail. You just said because we are going there next and this was facilitated by the people that we were meeting. Could you try to find out how this was done, how this was prepared, and who was facilitating this.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly who it was who had arranged it. But certainly, we were accompanied throughout our stay for the two-day period by the gentleman from Pale. I think he was probably the common denominator certainly between Manjaca and the meeting with Dr. Stakic and Trnopolje. There was no doubt that we were going straight after the meeting with Dr. Stakic then to see Trnopolje. But I would hate, ten years later, to try and say specifically who it was around the table who went with us, if anybody, other than the gentleman from Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Easily to be understood, no doubt. In your statement of 16th March of the year 2000, you mentioned inter alia, when discussing the "open reception centre of Trnopolje" guards in the facility wore some sort of military uniform. Could you please explain what is your understanding of this sort of military uniform? Do you remember? Do you still remember camouflage uniforms, were there certain military ranks showing -- indicated there or something else? I have to ask. But please try to tell us what is your recollection, what did you see, what kind of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: At this stage, I wish I have taken a photograph. It would have been far easier. They were wearing, I think, green. It could have been camouflaged, but certainly uniform. I can't remember what the unit designations were that they were wearing. I'm sure that -- I'm pretty certain that the chap who was in charge would have had rank insignia on him. I can't remember what he was. I certainly don't want to try and say he was this rank or that rank. What was quite clear is that they were wearing a uniform as opposed to being in civilian clothes, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this fair answer. In the same statement, you said inter alia, mentioning that there was a machine-gun post facing into the camp, and then you added: "And there were empty cartridge cases laying on the road." To be quite sure, because it's totally easily understood that it's difficult to have in the year 2000 the same recollection as you had it immediately after a meeting one or two days later, but was it on purpose that you mentioned these empty cartridge cases lying on the road, and why?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned it deliberately. I mentioned it because it struck me as remarkable that on a road which was running right next to a camp in which several thousand people were living, at a distance closer than I am to you now, that there should be empty cartridge cases where somebody had obviously been shooting. It was not at all clear where they had been shooting, but highly unlikely that somebody would have picked up empty cases and brought them to drop on the road. And I thought at the time that it was worth comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But no doubt it's your recollection you saw these empty cartridges beside --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. In one of your earlier statements, on the Banja Luka second visit, 25 August, 1992, it starts that "A Mr. Radic made a strong opening attack. Radic, did you get permission from the Bosanska Krajina government to arrange this visit? If not, why not?" Would it be correct to say that in the beginning of the line of visit, you faced strong opposition?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that what he was doing was trying very forcefully to put us in a position where we had to make a statement that would recognise the government, and at that point we were unable to recognise the government formally. And so he was trying forcefully to push us into a position where we would say something which he could then use to say, "Well, the ECMM has recognised us." I think that was what going on, as opposed to him being displeased that we were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. And finally, from my point of view, if you would have to describe to a third person the personality of Dr. Stakic, even though you only saw him for a very limited time, what was your personal impression of this Dr. Stakic? You can see him in the courtroom right now. What was the personality? Was there something special, a special impression, strong or more moderated person? Please feel free to describe what comes in your mind.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Very hard. I think that he was clearly -- he understood exactly what he was talking about. He was very lucid. If I say "cheerful," he was -- he wasn't laughing and chirping about the subject matter but he was a positive character. Under different circumstances, you could imagine having an interesting conversation with him, so a pleasant person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for helping us understand the entire environment better. It was of great assistance. Judge Fassi Fihri, please. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Witness, on several occasions, you have expressed your skepticism regarding the veracity of the Serbian version of events. You told us about two versions of events, and you expressed a certain opinion about the Serbian version as being false to a certain extent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Have you expressed your doubts to your interlocutories, even be it in a diplomatic way?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: On that occasion, I was not the person who was conducting the conversation, so I think that Sir John, who was leading the conversation on our side was very gently saying -- JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Did any member of the delegation? Did any one of you express your doubts?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that Sir John was making the point that if they wanted to be part of Western Europe and if they wanted to be following what they said they wanted to be doing, then the route was through a political dialogue as opposed to conflict. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can you also tell us whose suggestion it was to go to Trnopolje and Manjaca? Who was it who proposed these two camps for your visit?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that this was something that was being discussed at the London Conference and so I simply don't know who it was who identified as those being the two places for us to go to. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Who asked you to do that? Who was it who asked you to go there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: A request was put to the head of the ECMM by the CSCE to ask whether the ECMM could facilitate the visit. And as a result of that request, because we had already been into Banja Luka a couple of times, we agreed that we had the ability to take the rapporteur mission in. But I think that the agenda for the visit, so the locations of where we were going, had been arranged at a level above the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may help if I explain that there is a full report on the mission which will be dealt with by Mr. Mayhew, who is more intimately involved in it, and that will explain how the camps were chosen. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Were you aware of the existence of Omarska and Keraterm camps?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I had certainly heard about Omarska, and I was aware that it was further east, so towards Banja Luka, from Trnopolje, but we didn't go there. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Is it the case that you didn't think of going there, you were not aware of it, or -- ? Because you said that you raised the issue with Dr. Stakic and he was the one who told you that he knew of the existence of these two camps. So how was it actually? If you don't have any answer, you can feel free to say, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I'm not sure. JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, while insisting not to call the existing detention facilities as "camps," did Dr. Stakic acknowledge the very existence of these detention facilities in the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what is your impression of Dr. Stakic's in connection with these camps, their management and administration, in the light of your statement that "in all parts of former Yugoslavia at that time, there was a joint military and political command structure"? I quoted from your written statement made on 16 of March, year 2000, page 2, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that he would have been aware that the camps were there. He would have known exactly what was going on in terms of setting them up. He would have been a party to the decision-making process which led, I think, to the events which ended up with people being put into the camps. He would have been a party, I should think, to the discussions about what to do with the people who were in the camps. I don't think that he would have had day-to-day responsibility for the management of the camps because it struck me that that was in the hands of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any additional questions? JUDGE FASSI FIHRI: [Interpretation] Do you know Dr. Stakic who is here? Is it the same person that you had an opportunity to meet? Would you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, I have to give the opportunity to the parties. Any additional questions emanating from the questions of the Judges? The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we're going to go first, yes, I do have a couple areas I'd like to cover, Your Honour. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I emphasise very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Further cross-examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 32 of your original note, sir, in the top portion there seems to be something written in the Cyrillic and Latin script, if you will. Now, can you tell us if you wrote that in the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I certainly did not write it, because I'm not proficient in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who wrote that in the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: It was whoever was sitting to my right. And it may have been the gentleman from Pale, but I can't remember at this stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who wrote under the Cyrillic script in the Latin script the name "Milomir Stakic"?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think it was the same person because having had it written out in Cyrillic, I said, "This means nothing to me," so they then wrote it out in Latin so that I could understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us where in any of the documents that you prepared, either the original text, the report, or in the statement that you provided to the ICTY in March of 2000, where the word "Keraterm" appears? Because you gave a little testimony about the knowledge or the purported knowledge of Dr. Stakic as it may relate to the Keraterm camp. Can you tell us where that actually appears in any of those documents?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think I was asked whether I had any knowledge of that camp, and I didn't make any comment about that camp. So to be quite clear, we talked about Trnopolje. We talked about Omarska. And I'm not aware of the other camp, and I don't think it appears anywhere in my data.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the only time that Omarska appears is on the item that you and I discussed where you essentially verbatim write that Dr. Stakic states: "We have heard about Omarska," in essence. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nowhere else does it appear in either your original notes or in the report that you made or in the March 16th, 2000, interview that you gave to the ICTY. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also testified regarding your -- the difference between Manjaca and Keraterm -- strike that. That's where I'm ... You also discussed an issue relating to the description of Manjaca and Trnopolje. Is it fair to state that in March -- is it fair to state that in March in the year 2000, when you were being interviewed by the ICTY and the OTP, that you had your notes and your reports with you during that interview?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that statement that you gave them, under oath, that you signed, you, in fact, describe in some detail the differences, if you will, between Manjaca and Trnopolje. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, in that interview, although I tried to share some of the issues with you in that, you clearly state that they are quite different. One had barbed wire around it; namely, Manjaca. On the other hand, Trnopolje did not. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One had exclusively men in it; namely, Manjaca. And Trnopolje was, as you say, mixed age and gender. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think we have picked up on the point about the age and gender, and I think that I have come back and said that in practice, since my report says it was mostly men, it was probably mostly men, but your point is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, you also described some of the living conditions between Manjaca and Trnopolje. Correct? There was a difference between the two. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also, sir, described, perhaps indirectly, the emotion experienced by the men in Manjaca and the people in Trnopolje, namely, that the people in Manjaca were deadpan in their view; yet, on the other hand, the people in Trnopolje were free to walk around and were -- came up to you immediately and engaged in conversations with you as others gathered along. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm not clear how it arises out of Your Honours' questions. It just seems to me it's a repetition of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may reply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand it as the attempt of the Defence to contest what was said by the witness already before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I mean, Your Honour. I mean, we're going back to what was said in chief. And I thought this was meant to be matters arising from Your Honours' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Emanating from our questions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, on this, I believe the witness, and the record will bear it out, that he said, in fact, "There is a little difference between the two camps." That came from a question from the Chamber in connection with that, and I'm merely trying to clarify his view when he stated that there was very little difference between the two camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think the underlying facts were already several times adduced to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I then have the question for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, which was it? Was it the statements that you gave in your March 2000 report, that they are accurate, or is it as you've just testified today, that there was very little difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I ask you finally, if I may, you testified about what you thought what Dr. Stakic could or would have been responsible for. Do you know, sir, as you sit here whether or not in fact he was responsible in any shape or form in connection with the management or administration of Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: As I said, that's what I would surmise, as opposed to what I know for a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the basis of your --

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: Talking to parties on each of the sides and having dealings with Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the military and the political people on each of the sides, the way that people were structuring their affairs at that time, given that there was a war, it would be that you would have a joint command structure where the military and the politicians would be talking to each other and taking joint decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you don't know if that was actually what occurred in the Prijedor Municipality, do you? And that is just something that you surmise and speculate upon based upon your general understanding of other areas in the former Yugoslavia. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES MCLEOD
utterances.text: I think that's exactly what I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any additional questions? That's not the case. I have only to announce before concluding that I learned from the registry a mistake was made as regards the numbers of the evidence admitted under D. As D14 was already attributed in the past, the three documents admitted into evidence today have the numbers D15, 16, and 17. So this was this clarification. Then, it remains for me to thank you for this undertaking. I know it's really difficult, but I think also having present your original documents and the notes you took at the time, it's of utmost importance. And be sure that for both parties, but also for the decision of the Judges, it's incredibly important to have not only the witness statement, but the basis your notes at that time. And this should be a lesson to be learned for the future, that it's important to have these documents available because we all know how misleading our recollections sometimes, unfortunately, is. And therefore thank you very much for all your efforts. And this concludes the hearing for today. And we resume tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
